KEY MESSAGE 1...
A frontal zone over the region will become even more pronounced 
today. Upper flow will steadily increase through the day, with 
a couple waves passing through to interact with the temperature 
gradient zone. Precipitable water values, after stepping back a 
bit overnight, will ramp back up a bit with a lead shortwave in 
the morning and then top off approaching 2.50 inches with a 
stronger wave by this evening. Undercutting these waves aloft, 
will be the light southeast flow encroaching at the surface, 
advancing around high pressure over New England to push in some 
marine layer. So there will indeed be a gradient of conditions 
for the area, with highs ranging form only upper 60s-lower 70s 
Poconos-Catskills to lower-mid 80s in Finger Lakes. 

With the lead shortwave, there is considerable uncertainty for 
whether it will generate and sustain a line of convection/for how 
long. Some convection allowing models (CAMS) allow it to bring a 
decaying line of convection into the region during the morning. It 
will be driven by aloft-processes instead of being surface-based, so 
the severe risk may be limited. However, on the mesoscale we will 
have to see if it generates renewed convection with boundaries on 
the way out, which could lead to isolated strong to severe.

Wednesday afternoon, convective available potential energy (CAPE) 
climbs in a warm and very humid environment. As with yesterday, 
there may be a lack of triggers between waves. However, this time a 
stronger wave in projected to enter the area late afternoon through 
evening which will harness whatever CAPE builds up before then. 
Convective parameters especially more comfortably on the warm side 
of the frontal zone appear quite concerning late Wednesday. Surface-
rooted storms that fire with the wave will then ride up the shallow 
warm front, with time becoming more elevated. However, shallow warm 
fronts can be quite problematic with the shear that they generate in 
the low levels. There will be an overlapping zone of elevated 
helicity, which is why isolated tornadoes cannot be ruled out in 
addition the downburst potential from storm cores. Mitigating 
factors are limited midlevel temperature lapse rates as thermal 
profiles approach moist-adiabatic, and the trend towards a later 
arrival of the wave which is less able to harness diurnal heating. 
Latest guidance continues a sharp CAPE gradient along the I81 
corridor in NY and Northern PA. This gradient may once again be
the focus of the edge of strong/severe storms such as was the 
case Tuesday evening. 

Though the parade-route of passing shortwaves gradually presses 
south into Thursday, it is still close enough to pose a threat for 
stronger thunderstorms at least in Northeast PA, and elevated 
showers-embedded thunder farther north across the rest of the
region.

KEY MESSAGE 2... 

With a stalled front and high precipitable water values 
through Thursday morning of 2+ inches, potential for locally 
heavy rain and at least isolated flash flooding is a concern. 
Though there will be a gradient of severe weather parameters 
that lessens east of I-81, the parameters for excessive rainfall
will exist well north and east of the frontal zone in addition 
to along it. Warm cloud depths will be quite high, above 12kft 
agl, and a very moist low level jet will keep feeding in 
moisture. The High-Resolution Ensemble Forecast (HREF) model 
suite probability matched mean continues to depict stripes of 
2-3 inches. Even though exact locations could change, there in 
increasing confidence in the scenario leading to excessive 
rainfall amounts somewhere within our general area. Conjunction 
of parameters puts more of the focus on Central NY to Northern 
Tier of PA versus points farther south. Timing of waves, and 
frontal zone location at those times, will be key for who ends 
up with flash flooding, with potential for isolated amounts 
above 3 inches. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...

After the busier pattern through Thursday, the extended Labor
Day Weekend actually looks pretty benign. Friday into early 
next week, the large ridge in the central US retrogrades west 
with the trough in the northeast nudging into the mid Atlantic. 
This will help the flow become more northerly with seasonably 
cooler and drier air advecting in. Depending on how cool the 
850mb temperatures are, there could be some lake effect rain 
showers to deal with at times but for the most part the weekend
into early next week is looking mostly dry. We will be back to
fresh nights with lows of upper 40s-mid 50s, and highs of 
mainly 70s.
